sections.html:
• Name: Skunk Cleaner shrimp
  • Other names: Cleaner shrimp, White-striped cleaner shrimp, White banded clear shrimp, Skunk shrimp, Red Skunk Cleaner shrimp, Ambon Cleaner shrimp, Doctor shrimp
  • Scientific name: Lysmata amboinensis
  • Minimum tank size: 90 litres
  • Breeding: Difficult
  • Water type: SG = 1.023–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore/Carnivore
  • Temperament: Peaceful
  • Life span: up to 3 years
  • Colour: Amber with red stripes running down the centre
In Australia, its range extends from the Coral Sea (east coast of North Queensland) to Seal Rocks in northern New South Wales. There are reports of this species in Jeju-do Island in southern Korea.

These shrimp occur in tropical waters at low population densities and establish a cleaning symbiotic relationship with fishes, removing parasites, bacteria and damaged tissues.

They can be found in coral reef systems (usually around the 20-metre mark) of the Indo-West Pacific.

Skunk Cleaner shrimp are very laid-back shrimp. They are easy to keep and do not require special attention or care. Since the cleaner shrimp is naturally a reef invertebrate, its needs are nearly the same as most reef species: a temperature between 24 and 28°C, a KH of 8–12, and a pH between 8.1 and 8.4. In addition, these shrimp need a tank of more than 90 litres to thrive.

Regular water checks and maintenance create a good, liveable space for your Skunk Cleaner shrimp. Do not forget to do water changes, as they cannot live in high nitrate levels.

It is also recommended to have a rock that they can climb or perch upon, acting as a sort of car wash for your fish. Fish will swim up to them and await a generous cleaning. It keeps them healthy and bacteria-free and is also an amazing thing to watch.

Important: before putting them in your tank, do not forget to acclimate them.

The cleaner shrimp feed on parasites and dead skin on client fish as well as detritus. They will eat nearly any meaty type of fish food that you put in the tank, just be sure they are getting enough themselves. It is even suggested that you focus on feeding them directly so they are not left out.

Basically, their diet is made up of meaty seafood or marine flake food.

This species is a "low density" or "pairs" species. The cleaner shrimp, as the name suggests, is mainly known for its cleaning properties as it can clean parasites from fish skin, and even the mouth of a large fish like a grouper.

According to experiments, Skunk Cleaner shrimp can play a vital role in preventative care against parasites of ornamental fish. The beneficial services of Lysmata amboinensis extend beyond symbiosis with fish and include removal of all off-host life stages of marine parasites.

In one experiment, they consumed free-swimming eggs and larvae of a harmful parasite in the aquarium (for example, Neobenedenia sp.):

  • Under diurnal conditions, they consumed 65% of Neobenedenia eggs present in aquaria during the 12 h experimental period.
  • Under nocturnal conditions, the cleaner shrimp ate 15% of eggs.
  • They also reduced the abundance of free-swimming larvae by 25%.

By continuing with non-symbiotic cleaning behaviour, cleaner shrimp would continue to reduce the overall parasite load of the system and mitigate the incidence of reinfection. Cleaner shrimp were especially efficient at removing parasite eggs during the day.

Of the common shrimp kept in tanks, the Blood Shrimp (L. debelius), Peppermint Shrimp (L. wurdemanni) and Skunk Cleaner Shrimp (L. amboinensis), the Skunk Cleaner Shrimp is the most reliable, temperate and consistent in cleaning fish and maintaining a happy equilibrium in the tank. The other species do a decent enough job, but L. amboinensis is the best option.

Sexing and moulting

In Lysmata amboinensis, sexing and moulting (the way they routinely cast off an old exoskeleton) go hand in hand because this species is a protandric simultaneous hermaphrodite. At first they develop as males and then change to simultaneous hermaphrodites. As a result, they can function as both sexes during a reproductive cycle. So an inter-moult shrimp (functioning as a male) is able to mate with a newly moulted shrimp (playing the female role). The "male" will breed with the one that has moulted ("female") and fertilise the eggs.

Skunk Cleaner Shrimp become sexually mature (as a male) at a total length of 34.0 mm. In general, the mean inter-moult period ranges from 18–20 days. They act as males in the middle of the inter-moult cycle and as females immediately after moulting.

Paired shrimp moult and reproduce in a staggered synchronisation. They start moulting midway through their partner's inter-moult period. This ensures that individuals do not moult and reproduce as females at the same time, so that individuals will be ready to fertilise their partners. This allows a pair to reproduce every 10–12 days.

All shrimp species need adequate calcium supplement and trace minerals in the moulting process.

Tankmates

Lysmata amboinensis are very peaceful shrimp, so keeping them in any marine tank should be fine, as long as they are not placed with aggressive creatures that may attempt to eat or kill them, such as predatory shrimp, crabs or fish (like hawkfish and lionfish). Although these fish will use the cleaner shrimp for cleaning, there is always the chance they will also gulp the shrimp down.

If there are fish they identify as "predators" in the tank, they may advertise their cleaning services to these fish first and most often, so as to form a mutual agreement: they keep them clean and parasite free so long as they aren't eaten. According to experiments, Lysmata amboinensis alters its behaviour in the presence of potentially predatory clients by signalling more frequently or intensely to predatory clients than to non-predatory clients.

High density and aggression

Do not keep many Skunk Cleaner shrimp in small tanks; it can cause aggression. In confined space, one pair can attack and kill other shrimp.

In one experiment, selective mortality was observed in the triplet (45-litre tank) and quartet treatments (60-litre tank). After 42 days, one shrimp in each triplet and two shrimp in each quartet treatment had died. In all cases, shrimp died (in aggressive interactions) shortly after moulting. No mortality occurred in single and pair treatments.

Mating

Unlike most shrimp species, Skunk Cleaner Shrimp are not very active during mating. They usually do not display obvious pre-copulation behaviour and take significantly longer to transfer spermatophores and lay eggs after mating. Male-role shrimp often do not mate with newly moulted female-role shrimp immediately after detecting them. This behaviour may be at least partly caused by social environments (low density and low competition).

According to observations:

  • Moulting lasts 5–70 s
  • Copulation lasts 6–20 s
  • Mating takes place within 0–280 s (77.0 ±78.8 s). Of 15 replicates, only in one case did mating take place immediately (<1 second) after the female-role shrimp moulted; for the rest, mating occurred within 35–280 s after moulting.

In other shrimp species, males do not wait and mating often takes place even during the moulting process.

Breeding

Aquarium-based captive breeding of ornamental species can provide an alternative to wild collection, alleviate pressure on coral reefs, and satisfy growing market demand. Unfortunately, breeding Skunk Cleaner shrimp is extremely difficult due to the prolonged duration of larval development, punctuated by periods of high mortality. Besides documented laboratory studies, only a few people in the world have managed to breed a small number of them.

Mark Wunsch (Bangor) was the first to raise Lysmata amboinensis, in 1996, and wrote his doctoral thesis on it. Out of 2,150 larvae, he could raise only one to settle, after 142 days.

Some facts about breeding

  • Depending on the temperature, incubation lasts approximately 10–12 days (at a water temperature of 24–27°C).
  • The infertile eggs produced by a single shrimp disappear within 4 days.
  • Females have very long intervals from mating to egg laying (9 hours).
  • A hatch can range from 30 to 2000 larvae, but usually ranges from 300 to 1650.
  • Fecundity is positively correlated with female body length. However, parasitism, stress, temperature and diet can also affect reproductive output in decapods. For example, 100% cover of a 42.9 mm shrimp would hold 1144 eggs, of a 44.2 mm 1297, of a 46.2 mm 1532, of a 48.3 mm 1779, and of a 49.6 mm 1932 eggs.
  • Maturation diets have been shown to affect fecundity and offspring quality. The common practice in shrimp culture is the use of fresh frozen foods supplemented with artificial diets, such as squid, mussel, polychaetes and Artemia biomass, with artificial diets used only as a supplement.
  • The colour of the embryo gradually changes during development from light green, dark green, dark yellow, to tawny.
  • Embryos hatch as planktonic larvae termed zoeae.
  • The number of stages a larva undergoes prior to settling is 14.
  • The larval period is up to 150 days.
  • In captivity, larval food quality and quantity, cannibalism and inappropriate stocking densities have been shown to be important factors determining larval survival.
  • Hydroids are a real danger. They are very hard to get rid of, so the best method is to move the larvae into a clean tank.

Rearing set-up

To raise larvae you will need a separate tank with a water temperature of 28°C, pH 8.1–8.4 and salinity of 35 ‰. Moults, uneaten food and waste should be removed before the next feeding.

Several feeding and zootechnical experiments were conducted under laboratory conditions to test the effect of food during the first day post-hatch, the effect of feeding with microalgae on larval digestion 24 h post-hatch, the effect of enriched rotifers on survival, and the combined effect of stocking density and food concentration on growth and survival of young larvae. According to the results:

  • Enriched Artemia (with commercial products) had high reproductive output at all spawns. For example, the minimum number of larvae was 49 (± 11) and the maximum was 529 (± 76), recorded for the "not enriched" and "enriched" diets respectively.
  • Enriched rotifers result in higher larval survival during the first days of life compared with larvae fed non-enriched rotifers, and survival does not depend on the relation between larval density and food concentration. Enriched rotifers can be an alternative to Artemia only during the first 3 days of life.
  • A stocking density of 10 larvae per ml showed higher survival than a density of 20 larvae per ml.
  • Larval survival can be significantly improved if live food is given throughout the first day of life. After hatching, larvae rely on egg yolk reserves, which may not be sufficient for the first 24 h of life.
  • In spite of the conspicuous carnivorous feeding strategy, larvae may also swallow microalgae immediately after hatching. In some cases Tetraselmis chuii and Chaetoceros gracilis were used. However, microalgae alone are not enough to support growth or survival during larval development.

Larval stages

During the prolonged larval phase, mortality is very high. The larval cycle has 14 zoeal stages, which last about 70 days. After that, it takes about another 70 days to metamorphose into a copy of the adult. At metamorphosis, larvae can reach 2–2.5 cm in length. Unfortunately, only a small percentage of larval batches survive to the juvenile stage.

Skunk Cleaner shrimp is a popular ornamental shrimp known for its bright colours and striking patterns. They have a beautiful yellow colour with two bright red stripes along their back, and a streak of white in the middle. The tip of the tail is red and has four white spots.

They grow to be about 5–6 cm total length, so they don't take up a huge amount of space. However, their long white antennae (through which they sense the environment) need space to flourish and keep your fish parasite free.

Reef safety: as long as you keep up with their food, there is no danger of them ruining your corals.

Many hobbyists have noted that they will steal all the food from the corals. However, this can be solved simply by feeding them regularly.
